Hello and welcome to The Insight by Oak Tree Capital.
I'm Anna Schumansky, Oakry's senior financial writer, and today we have something a little bit different for you.
We've put together three excerpts from Oak Tree's recent client conference.
First up, we have co-chairman Howard Marks, who will set the stage with his discussion about the massive changes we've been seeing in financial markets in recent years.
We'll then hear from members of Oak Tree's global credit team who will explain how these changes are impacting performance.
performing credit. And finally, you'll hear from Oak Tree's global opportunities team who'll discuss today's

significant, and potentially long-lasting, not your normal garden variety short-term fluctuation.
And as I said in further thoughts, largely thanks to highly accommodative monetary policy,
we went through an unusually easy time in a number of important regards over a prolonged period,
but that time is over. And that is our belief, and we believe at Oak Tree that we are in a fundamentally

a loan outstanding from the bank, and the interest rate was 22 and a quarter.
Forty years later, in 2020, I was able to borrow at two and a quarter fixed for 15 years, and I

important single financial event of the last half century. Not the bankruptcy of
Lehman, not the meltdown of the tech bubble or Black Monday. This was really important, but I
I think few people recognize it as such because it took so long and occurred so
gradually.

I believe that a significant amount of money that was made over that period was
because of the tailwind provided by the massive drop in interest rates.
Declining interest rates have a number of very salutary effects.
They stimulate the economy.
They increase consumer demand by making time purchases cheaper.
Thus, they make money.
most businesses more profitable.
They make assets more valuable by reducing the discount rate that is applied to future cash flows.
They reduce the cost of capital and make financing more accessible, and they make default and bankruptcy less likely.
And from 2010, for example, to 2019, we had a default rate on high-yield bonds that
averaged 1% a year, whereas the historic average is close to 4%.
So very, very profound impact.

to the end of 21, when it gave up on inflation being transitory and decided to raise interest rates,
which it did in early 22.
Now, when I did the rate,
research, I was surprised to find that over this 13-year period, I think the Fed funds rate
